chunks.title: Welcome to Replit Learn
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit Learn
Build with confidence.
A practical learning path from a blank idea to a production-ready application.
Learn how Replit projects fit together, how the Workspace supports your work, and how to build, publish, and share an app.

chunks.title: Welcome to Build
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Maybe you’ve been dreaming of an app of your own: a personal project, a business idea, or something useful to share with friends and family. Perhaps you’ve even started, but finding the time to bring all the pieces together has been the tricky part.
Replit helps you turn that idea into an app using natural language. Describe what you want in your own words, then use Replit to bring it to life. You can build, test, and publish in one place. You bring the direction, try the result, and decide what to improve.
You don’t need to master the underlying infrastructure, the systems that keep an app running, before you begin. This course introduces the building blocks one at a time, then helps you put them to work in an app you can share.
Build is about more than getting your first app on the screen. It’s a path toward becoming a power builder: someone who understands how an app’s building blocks work together and can use that understanding to make better decisions. You’ll practice describing what you need, testing what Replit creates, and improving your app step by step. That understanding helps you tackle more ambitious ideas with confidence.
Already a developer? Some of these concepts will be familiar. Feel free to skim the basics and focus on how the pieces fit together in Replit, and how Replit can support your existing workflow.
Describe what the Build course will help you practice
Explain your role when building with Replit
Choose a small app idea to explore as you learn
When you’re ready to explore your idea, you could ask Replit: “I want to build a simple app for [someone] to [do something]. Help me plan a small first version, and explain any unfamiliar terms.” Review the plan before asking Replit to build it.

chunks.title: Welcome to Build
chunks.heading: What you’ll learn
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Build takes you from understanding an app to creating, sharing, and improving one. The course follows four connected parts:
App foundations: get to know interfaces, code, data, access, and the connections that make an app work.
Build with Replit: describe what you need, make changes, test the result, and publish a working version.
Secure and monitor: protect your app and understand what happens when people use it.
Grow and scale: learn from feedback, help people find your app, and prepare it for more activity.

chunks.title: Welcome to Build
chunks.heading: Start with something small enough to try
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Your idea doesn’t need to be a business or a big launch. A family recipe collection, a booking tool, or a small improvement to an existing app is a useful starting point. Choose one thing you want someone to be able to do. You can add more once that first piece works.

chunks.title: Welcome to Build
chunks.heading: Build your understanding as you go
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Read an explanation, try a small change, and look at what happened. You can ask Replit to explain unfamiliar code or an error in plain language. You don’t have to write every line yourself, but you’ll learn enough to ask better questions and check the result. If something doesn’t work the first time, that gives you something specific to investigate.

chunks.title: Welcome to Build
chunks.heading: Make the course fit your starting point
chunks.text:
App Foundations
New to building apps? Follow the lessons in order and take your time with App foundations. Already comfortable with software development? Skim familiar concepts and spend more time on the Replit workflows that are new to you. Discover Replit is available for broader orientation, but you don’t need to finish it before starting Build.

chunks.title: Welcome to Build
chunks.heading: Your first step
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Write down who your app could help and one thing it could help them do. You can change your mind later. This is a starting point, not a commitment. Next, “What is an app?” connects familiar everyday apps to the building blocks you’ll use.

chunks.title: What is an app?
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You probably use apps every day to message friends, check the weather, or book something in your browser. But what makes something an app? At its simplest, an app is software that helps someone do something.
In this lesson, you’ll build a personal recipe app with Replit. You’ll add, edit, and find recipes, then explore the building blocks that make it work.
Explain what an app is
Recognize the different building blocks of an app
Build your first app on Replit
Try the recipe prompt above in Replit. In Preview, add a recipe, edit an ingredient, and search for it by name. Refresh the page to check that it is still there in the same browser. If something doesn’t work as expected, describe what you tried and what happened to Replit. Each small check helps you turn your idea into an app you can rely on.

chunks.title: What is an app?
chunks.heading: Apps can live on your phone or in your browser
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Think of Spotify for music, WhatsApp for messages, or Google Calendar for planning your week. Each helps you do something different. App is short for application. Some apps are installed on a phone or computer. Others open through a link in a browser, and many offer both options.
Illustration of Spotify showing the same Everyday favorites playlist in a laptop browser and a mobile app.
One app, different screens. AI-generated illustration of Spotify, not a product screenshot.
/images/spotify-browser-mobile.png

chunks.title: What is an app?
chunks.heading: Let’s build your first app
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Let’s build a little recipe book just for you. You’ll be able to add your favorite recipes, edit the ingredients, and find something to cook. Start simple: no accounts or sharing yet, just a useful app of your own. With Replit, you can describe what you want in plain English or another language you speak. That’s what natural language means: your own words, rather than code. Here’s the request you’ll use:
Create a personal recipe app where I can add, edit, and find my favorite recipes. Include a recipe name, ingredients, and instructions. Keep it simple and save my recipes in this browser. No sign-in needed.
That description is called a prompt. Replit uses it to create the code that makes your app work. You can try the result and ask for changes as you go. Let’s look at what happens behind the scenes.

chunks.title: What is an app?
chunks.heading: What did Replit make?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Your prompt describes an experience. Behind the scenes, Replit creates the interface, the logic that responds to your actions, and a way to remember your recipes. For this first version, those pieces can all run in your browser. The frontend is the part you see and interact with. Its user interface, or UI, includes the recipe list, form, and buttons.
The interface turns “add, edit, and find” into controls you can use, such as a recipe form, an Edit button, and a search field.
The app’s logic responds to those controls. When you select Save, it can check that you entered a title, then add the recipe or update an existing one.
Browser storage remembers the recipes in this browser on this device, even after you close the page. Clearing that storage can erase them, and they won’t automatically appear on another device.

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You’ve described your recipe app in a prompt: a request that tells Replit what you want to create. While the app is being built for you, let’s explore how that prompt becomes a first version you can open and try.
The good news with Replit is that you can get started without knowing how to write code. Replit handles that work, while you decide what your app should do and check that the result matches your needs. A simple first version can take minutes. More ambitious apps need more time, testing, and refinement.
This lesson explains the process of building an app. Follow progress in chat or open your project in Replit. Chat will notify you when it receives the completed build update.
Explain how Replit turns your prompt into code and an interface
Test a first version in Preview
Request a specific improvement and test the result again

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: First, your prompt becomes a task
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Your recipe prompt sets the goal and the boundaries: add, edit, and find recipes, save them in this browser, and leave out sign-in. Replit uses those details to decide what the first version needs. A clear prompt helps keep the work focused.

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: Your app starts with instructions
chunks.text:
App Foundations
When you save a recipe, the app takes what you typed and adds it to your collection. When you search for an ingredient, it finds matching recipes. Neither action happens by itself: the app follows written instructions. Those instructions are called code. Replit writes that code and saves it in files.
Some instructions describe what appears on the screen. Others describe what happens when you select a button or save a recipe.
Together with images, settings, and other resources, these files make up the project for your app. You don’t need to read every line to start exploring what it does.

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: Replit creates the parts you see and use
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Think about opening your recipe app. You see recipe cards, type into a search field, and select a button to add a recipe. These visible, interactive parts are its user interface, or UI. Replit writes the code that brings them to life in your browser. This browser-side part of the app is called the frontend.
To put those pieces on the page, web apps use HTML for structure, CSS for appearance, and JavaScript for behavior. For example, the recipe heading needs structure, the card needs styling, and the search field needs instructions to filter recipes.
Replit may organize that code with a framework, a set of tools for building an app. You don’t need to learn these languages or tools before getting started. For now, connect the names to the things you can see and try.
Understanding these building blocks gives you an advantage as a builder. You can give Replit more specific direction, such as changing the recipe cards’ appearance while keeping the saving behavior the same. That curiosity helps you become a power builder, one small discovery at a time. It is a way to grow, not a requirement for getting started.
For this first recipe app, the recipe logic and saved recipes also stay in the browser. It does not need an application backend, shared database, or family accounts.

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: Testing turns code into something you can try
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Replit starts the app, checks for problems, and can revise the code as it builds. A development server serves your web app to Preview, where you can see and test it. In this recipe app, the interface and recipe logic then run in your browser. A working Preview is not proof that every feature is correct.
Preview lets you compare the result with what you had in mind. Try the controls, notice what works, and describe anything that needs changing.
Preview is not the same as publishing a production version. Development links can still be accessible to others, so do not assume an unpublished app is private.

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: When it is ready, give it a small test
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Watch for the ready message in chat, then open your recipe app. Add a made-up recipe, edit it, and refresh to see whether it is still there. If something is wrong, describe what you tried and what happened. You do not need to diagnose the code yourself. Next, you’ll explore the project, code, and files behind that experience.

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: A first version is a starting point
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Your prompt describes a deliberately simple app, not every detail you might have in mind. Replit has to make choices about the details you leave open, so the result may not match everything you pictured. Ask for one specific improvement at a time, then test the change. That cycle is called iteration.

chunks.title: What is Replit building?
chunks.heading: Next, meet your project
chunks.text:
App Foundations
In Replit, a project brings together your code, resources, and the things you create. It can contain one app or several related outputs, called artifacts, such as a web app, mobile app, slide deck, or dashboard. Next, you’ll explore the project and files behind your recipe app.

chunks.title: Projects, code & files
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You’ve seen Replit build a first version of your recipe app. Behind that result, it wrote code and organized it into files and folders. Let’s open your project and see how those pieces fit together.
The good news is that these files are available for you to explore, but you don’t need to manage or edit them yourself. You can describe a change to Replit and let it update the code. For now, your goal is to recognize the organization, not understand every file.
Open your project’s Files panel
Explain how projects, artifacts, and files fit together
Describe a change to Replit without editing files yourself

chunks.title: Projects, code & files
chunks.heading: Open your project’s files
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Open the same recipe project you’ve been using. In the layout shown below, the Library control sits in the upper-right corner, next to Publish.
Open Library, then select the Files tab.
Expand the artifacts folder, then the recipe-box folder to explore this example.
Notice the folders and files alongside Preview. This list is called a file tree, like the folders on your computer. Your own project may use different names.
Recipe Box running in Preview beside the expanded Files panel, with the recipe-box folder selected inside artifacts.
The running app is in the center. Its project files are on the right. Open the image to enlarge the file tree.
/images/recipe-project-files.png

chunks.title: Projects, code & files
chunks.heading: See how Replit organized the work
chunks.text:
App Foundations
In this example, the artifacts folder contains three folders: api-server, mockup-sandbox, and recipe-box. The recipe-box folder is our starting point. Inside it, you can see source and public folders, along with files used to configure the app.
The other folder names suggest supporting server and preview tooling. Their presence alone does not tell you which features your recipe app uses. Replit can inspect their contents and explain their roles.
Outside that folder, you can also see lib, scripts, replit.md, and configuration files. You don’t need to learn every name now.
Some files contain code. Others hold images, written guidance, or settings. Together, they support the app you see in Preview.

chunks.title: Projects, code & files
chunks.heading: A project brings the pieces together
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Your recipe app is something you can build and publish. In Replit, an output like this is called an artifact. Other examples include a mobile app, a slide deck, or a dashboard. A project can contain one artifact or several related artifacts, together with their code, shared resources, and settings.
The project is the container for the work.
Artifacts are the outputs you create inside it.
Files and folders organize the code and resources that support those outputs. Not every folder is a separate artifact.

chunks.title: Projects, code & files
chunks.heading: Explore without managing every file
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You can open the files whenever you want to understand more. Looking at a file does not change the app, and you don’t have to edit its code to make improvements. Describe the result you want to Replit, then test the change in Preview.
For example, you can ask for clearer recipe titles without knowing which file controls their appearance.
If you’re curious, ask Replit which files it changed and why. Connecting those explanations to your project helps you become a more confident builder.
Next, you’ll explore the frontend and UI more closely, using the same recipe app.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
The recipe form, the Save button, and the list of things you want to cook are your app’s user interface. Let’s connect what you see to what makes it work.
Recognize the frontend and user interface
Explain the roles of structure, style, and interaction
Notice how an interface responds to an action

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Start with a button you recognize
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Ask Replit to show the code behind your recipe form. Then open the app from chat and find the form yourself. The details may differ, but the connection is the same: code becomes an interface you can use.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: What did Replit show you?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
The frontend runs in the browser. Its user interface, or UI, is the part you see and interact with. The code in chat connects the recipe fields and buttons to that visible experience.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Three jobs behind the screen
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You don’t need to write these languages to recognize their jobs. In a web app, they work together:
HTML provides structure, such as headings, labels, and buttons. React may describe that structure using a syntax called JSX.
CSS controls appearance, such as the space between recipe cards and the color of a button.
JavaScript handles interaction, such as filtering recipes when you type. TypeScript adds checks to JavaScript code.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: A helpful interface answers back
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Try saving a recipe in your app. Does the recipe appear? Does anything explain an empty title? Useful feedback makes the result clear. If feedback is missing, you have found a specific improvement, not failed the lesson. Next, you’ll follow the logic behind that action.

chunks.title: Backend & logic
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A button is only the start. When you select Save, your app follows instructions: check the recipe, update the collection, and remember the result. That is app logic.
Trace the logic behind saving a recipe
Explain why app logic does not always need a backend
Recognize work that belongs on a server

chunks.title: Backend & logic
chunks.heading: Follow one recipe
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Ask Replit to trace the Save action in your project. You are looking for a short story: what happens first, what happens next, and where the recipe ends up.

chunks.title: Backend & logic
chunks.heading: What did Replit show you?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Logic means the rules and steps the app follows. Checking a title, adding a recipe, and filtering a list are all logic. Your first recipe app can do these jobs in the browser. Logic does not automatically mean backend.

chunks.title: Backend & logic
chunks.heading: When does a backend help?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A backend is application code that runs on a server rather than in the reader’s browser. It can check permissions, work with shared data, or call a service using a secret. People can inspect and change browser code, so important access checks cannot rely on the interface alone.

chunks.title: Backend & logic
chunks.heading: A request connects the two
chunks.text:
App Foundations
For a future shared recipe collection, the interface could send a Save request to the backend. The backend would check access, save the recipe, and return a result. An API is the agreed way those parts exchange requests and responses. That is a possible next version, not a claim that your app already works this way. Next, you’ll explore where recipes are remembered.

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You save a recipe, close the page, and come back later. How does the app remember it? Let’s check where your first version keeps its recipes.
Identify where the recipe app currently saves data
Explain a database record using a recipe
Distinguish browser storage from shared data

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: Find out before adding more
chunks.text:
App Foundations
The original request asked for browser storage. Ask Replit to inspect what was actually created. The answer matters more than assuming the prompt was followed perfectly.

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: What did Replit show you?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Browser storage belongs to this app’s address in this browser. It can survive a refresh, but it does not automatically travel to another device. Clearing browser data can remove it. Use a made-up recipe when you test, not your only copy of a favorite.

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: A database gives information a shared home
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A database organizes information so an app can find and update it. A recipe can be a record with fields such as an ID, name, ingredients, and instructions. The ID distinguishes two recipes even if both are called Pancakes.

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: What about the family collection?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
To load recipes across devices, a later version could save them in a shared database. That does not automatically make them public or give family members permission. Access rules still matter. This lesson inspects your current storage; it does not migrate or erase your recipes. Next, you’ll consider recipe photos.

chunks.title: File storage
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A recipe name is text. A photo of your pancakes is a file. Your app can use both, but they have different storage needs.
Distinguish project files from uploaded files
Explain how a recipe can reference a photo
Identify checks needed before accepting uploads

chunks.title: File storage
chunks.heading: Does your app already have photos?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Ask Replit to check. A decorative image included with the project is not the same as an upload feature. It is completely fine if your simple recipe app has neither yet.

chunks.title: File storage
chunks.heading: What did Replit show you?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Project files help build the app. Uploaded files arrive when someone uses it. A photo saved later needs a durable home, not just a temporary file on the running server.

chunks.title: File storage
chunks.heading: Connect a photo to its recipe
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Object storage is designed to keep files such as images. A recipe record can store a reference to its photo while the image itself lives in file storage. Think of the reference as the address of the photo, not the photo itself.

chunks.title: File storage
chunks.heading: A useful upload has boundaries
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Before adding uploads, decide which file types and sizes are allowed, and who can view or remove them. A photo is not private just because its link is hard to guess. Your app needs to enforce access. Next, you’ll explore who should be allowed into the family recipe collection.

chunks.title: Users & access
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Your first recipe app was just for you. If you invite your family, the app needs to know who is visiting and what they are allowed to do.
Distinguish signing in from having permission
Choose simple access rules for shared recipes
Recognize that Learn sign-in is separate from app sign-in

chunks.title: Users & access
chunks.heading: Check what exists today
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Ask Replit to inspect access in your app. Your original prompt said no sign-in. Being signed into Learn or Replit does not mean the recipe app has its own family accounts.

chunks.title: Users & access
chunks.heading: What did Replit show you?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Authentication verifies identity: who is signing in? Authorization checks permission: may this person view or change this recipe? An app can recognize someone without granting them access to every collection.

chunks.title: Users & access
chunks.heading: Keep the first rules small
chunks.text:
App Foundations
For a future shared collection, you might let an owner invite family members and let members add recipes. Decide who can edit or delete someone else’s recipe. There is no need to invent ten roles when two explain the real responsibilities.

chunks.title: Users & access
chunks.heading: A hidden button is not protection
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Hiding Delete helps explain the interface, but it does not secure shared data. The backend must check permission when a request arrives. Family access is a future change to review and test, not something this inspection enables. Next, you’ll see how an app can connect to another service.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Imagine sending yourself a shopping list from your recipe app. Instead of building an email service, your app could connect to an existing one. That connection is an integration.
Explain an integration with a recipe app example
Identify where private service credentials belong
Describe a safe response when a service fails

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Look for connections
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Ask Replit which external services your app actually uses. A small browser-only recipe app may not need any. The activity also explores one possible addition without connecting an account or sending an email.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: What did Replit show you?
chunks.text:
App Foundations
An integration lets your app use a capability from another service. An API is how the two communicate. For a shopping-list email, the app would send selected ingredients and a recipient to an email service. Only send the information the task needs.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Keep private keys out of the browser
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Some services require a private API key, a credential that allows the app to make requests. Keep private keys in a protected server environment, not in browser code, lesson chat, or a public file. A backend can use the key without handing it to the person opening the app.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Plan for a missed delivery
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A service can be unavailable. Your app should say the email was not confirmed, preserve the shopping list, and offer a safe next step. It should not claim success because a button was pressed. When retries are needed, avoid sending duplicate emails.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: You have a map of your app
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You followed one recipe app from its files to its interface, logic, storage, access, and possible connections. You don’t need to remember every technical term. You now know what to ask, where to look, and what to check before adding more. That completes App foundations. The next module focuses on building and improving features.

chunks.title: Welcome to Replit
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Welcome! Whether you’re new to Replit or have built a few projects with it, this is a place to discover what you can do. Replit helps you explore information, get work done, and turn your ideas into apps.
For example, you can:
Research an idea, compare options, and check sources.
Summarize notes or find information in tools you choose to connect.
Schedule recurring tasks, such as a weekly update.
Turn an idea into a web app you can try and improve.
Explore different designs and create visual assets, such as images.
The good news is that you don’t need technical or coding experience to get started. You describe what you want, review the result, and ask Replit for improvements.
Before you begin, have these ready:
A Replit account you can sign into.
A Google account with Google Calendar that you’re allowed to connect to Replit. A personal or test account works well; a managed work or school account may need administrator approval.
Fictional party details for practice. Don’t include a child’s name, photo, or home address.
We’ll connect Google Calendar in “Connect your tools.” You don’t need to connect it before starting. Gmail is not required for this exercise, and you can read along without connecting an account.
Throughout this course, you’ll plan a child’s birthday party. Step by step, you’ll:
Brainstorm ideas and explore party themes.
Connect Google Calendar, then ask Replit to add the birthday event.
Create a shopping list of things to buy.
Build a website where guests can RSVP.
Design invitations and create supporting images.
You can use fictional details while practicing. Let’s get started!

chunks.title: Start with a chat
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
When you open Replit’s home screen, you’ll see a large composer, also called the prompt box.
It’s one of the main ways you interact with Replit. Everything starts with a chat where you explain what you want to achieve.
In this lesson, you’ll brainstorm birthday-party themes, choose one, and ask for a picture. Keep the same chat open so you can build on your ideas.
Use fictional details for this exercise. You don’t need to share a child’s name, photo, or exact location.
Write a prompt to brainstorm party themes
Choose a theme with a follow-up
Ask for an image to visualize your idea

chunks.title: Start with a chat
chunks.heading: Tell Replit what you have in mind
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Write your request in the prompt box. That request is a prompt. Start with the goal and a few helpful details. You’re just asking for ideas for now. You’ll ask for the website later.
I’m planning a birthday party for a six-year-old, with ten children in a park. Help me brainstorm four themes with simple activities.
Send the prompt in Replit and read the suggestions. Notice how your details give the ideas a direction. The answer may differ from someone else’s, and that’s fine.

chunks.title: Start with a chat
chunks.heading: Let’s choose a theme together
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Read Replit’s suggestions and explore the ideas you like. For the rest of this course, we’ll choose a Pokémon theme so our checklist, birthday app, and designs all follow the same story. Reply in the same chat to continue.
Let’s go with a Pokémon theme. Suggest three simple activities that fit it.
Read the activities and ask for a simpler option if you need one. You’re welcome to use your own theme, but the examples from here on will use Pokémon.

chunks.title: Start with a chat
chunks.heading: Picture the party
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Now ask for a picture of the theme you chose. You don’t need to repeat the whole plan in the same chat.
Create an image of what this birthday party could look like, with decorations and a picnic table in a park, using our chosen theme.
Look at the picture. Does it fit your idea? You can ask for one change, such as different colors or simpler decorations. That’s a chat: describe, review, and refine.

chunks.title: Connect your tools
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Connect Google Calendar to Replit so it can help with your schedule. In this lesson, you’ll use the Integrations page, sign in with Google, and review the calendar access you’re granting. You don’t need to connect Gmail or create an event yet.
Find Google Calendar in the Integrations page
Sign in with the intended Google account
Review calendar permissions before allowing access

chunks.title: Connect your tools
chunks.heading: Connect to Google Calendar
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Follow these five steps in Replit and Google. The screenshots have account details and private sidebar content removed. Your screen may look slightly different, especially if you already have a connection.

chunks.title: Connect your tools
chunks.heading: 1. Locate and open Integrations
chunks.text:
Replit 101
On Replit’s home screen, find Integrations in the left sidebar and click it. This opens the integration library shown below.
Replit integration library with Integrations selected in the left sidebar. Account details and private sidebar content are removed.

chunks.title: Use your tools
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Now that Google Calendar is connected, let’s use it. You’ll ask Replit to add a birthday event, review the details, and check the result in Google Calendar. This is a real action in a connected tool, not just a suggested plan.
Continue in your party-planning chat with Google Calendar connected. You don’t need Gmail for this activity, including calendar invitations.
The example uses fictional party details: September 22, 2026, from 3:00 to 5:00 PM in the Europe/Zurich time zone. Replace the date, year, time zone, and calendar name with the ones you intend to use. Choose a calendar where you’re allowed to create a test event.
Ask Replit to create a calendar event from a prompt
Review the details and verify the saved event
Understand how integrations let Replit act in connected tools

chunks.title: Use your tools
chunks.heading: 1. Ask Replit to add the birthday
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Copy the prompt below, or write it in your own words. Replace [calendar name] before sending it in Replit. Include a title, full date, start and end time, and time zone so Replit doesn’t have to guess. For this first try, don’t add guests or a private address.
Create an event called “Birthday party · practice” on September 22, 2026, from 3:00 to 5:00 PM, using the Europe/Zurich time zone, in my Google Calendar named [calendar name]. Add “Fictional birthday-party planning exercise” to the description. Show me the details before creating it and wait for my confirmation. Ask me if the calendar or any detail is unclear. Don’t add guests or send invitations.
Copying the prompt here does not send it or change your calendar. Paste it into Replit, edit the example details, and send it there.

chunks.title: Use your tools
chunks.heading: 2. Review and confirm
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Read the proposed event. Check the title, date and year, start and end time, time zone, and destination calendar. Correct anything that is wrong in the same chat. Once everything is right, ask Replit to create the event and review any approval card it shows.
Create the one birthday event we just reviewed, using the confirmed details and calendar. Don’t add guests or send invitations. Give me a link to the saved event.

chunks.title: Use your tools
chunks.heading: 3. Check the event in Google Calendar
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Open the returned event link or go to Google Calendar. Check that the event exists on the intended calendar at the correct date and time, and that it has no guests. A proposed event in chat is not the same as a saved event. If creation fails or the result is unclear, check your calendar before trying again so you don’t create duplicates. You can delete the practice event when you’re finished.

chunks.title: Use your tools
chunks.heading: Optional: invite your guests
chunks.text:
Replit 101
If you have the email addresses of people you intend to invite, you can ask Replit to add them to the existing event and send Google Calendar invitations. This uses Calendar, not Gmail. Invitations notify real people, so skip this during a fictional practice exercise. For a real party, replace the placeholders, check every address, and review the guest list before authorizing invitations.
For the existing birthday event we just created, prepare to invite [guest email addresses]. Show me the event and guest list first. Don’t add guests or send invitations until I confirm, and don’t create another event.
When the real guest list is correct, explicitly ask Replit to add those guests and send the calendar invitations. Review any approval card, then check the event’s guest list. An invitation is not an RSVP: guests still need to respond.

chunks.title: Use your tools
chunks.heading: What did the integration make possible?
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Without an integration, Replit can help write an event title, suggest a schedule, or draft an invitation. Connecting Google Calendar authorizes access to that service within the permissions you granted. Replit can then use Calendar’s tools to create or update an actual event when you ask. Your prompt describes the action; the integration provides access to the calendar; checking the saved event confirms the result.
Connection: you grant access to a particular Google account and its permitted calendar actions.
Request: you tell Replit what to do, with enough detail to avoid guessing.
Review: you check the proposed action, especially when it changes data or notifies others.
Result: you verify the change in Google Calendar, not just in the chat.

chunks.title: Create a checklist
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
We’ve brainstormed a party theme, connected our tools, and added the birthday to the calendar. Now let’s create the checklist together. Replit can search the web for supplies and help turn our ideas into a shopping list we can actually use.
Search the web for supplies that fit your party theme and budget
Check product links, prices, and delivery details
Create a checklist you can use to track purchases

chunks.title: Create a checklist
chunks.heading: 1. Find supplies for your theme
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Continue in the chat where you chose your theme. Maybe it’s dinosaurs, space, or something entirely different. Let’s find decorations, tableware, and games that fit. Copy this prompt, replace the brackets, and give Replit a budget and a country or region to shop in. There’s no need to share your home address.
Let’s find supplies for the birthday party we’ve been planning. Use our chosen theme, [number] guests, and a shopping budget of [amount and currency]. Search the web for decorations, plates and cups, and simple party-game supplies available in [country or region]. Suggest a few affordable options with product links, quantities, listed prices, and delivery information where available. Ask if the theme or party date is unclear, and flag anything you cannot verify. Don’t buy anything.

chunks.title: Create a checklist
chunks.heading: 2. Take a look at what Replit found
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Open a few of the product links. Do the items fit your theme? Are there enough plates for everyone? Check pack sizes, prices, shipping costs, and whether delivery is likely before the party. Prices and availability can change, so treat the results as shopping research, not a reservation. If something isn’t quite right, ask for a small change.
Keep the theme and guest count. Find a less expensive alternative for [item], and update the estimated total. Show the product link and flag any shipping costs or delivery dates you could not confirm.

chunks.title: Create a checklist
chunks.heading: 3. Turn your choices into a checklist
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Once you like the options, let’s put everything in one place. Keep the checklist in this chat so you can return to it as you prepare. We’ll use the same list in the next lesson to check your progress each week.
Turn the party supplies we chose into a checklist in this chat. Give each item an ID, quantity, product link, estimated cost, buy-by date, purchase status, and notes. Use “Not started,” “Ordered,” and “Delivered” for purchases, and don’t mark anything bought unless I’ve confirmed it. Add a separate preparation section for invitations and RSVPs, the cake, and planning games. Keep the total within our agreed budget, and show unknown costs separately. Ask about missing details rather than guessing. Don’t place orders or send invitations.
Already have the plates at home? Bought decorations in a shop? Tell Replit and ask it to update the notes. Your updates matter just as much as an email receipt.

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Our checklist is ready, and the party is getting closer. Let’s make it easier to keep track of what’s been bought and who’s coming. We’ll connect Gmail, then ask Replit to check for RSVP replies and purchase confirmations each week. That regular check-in is a Routine.
Use your existing checklist to track party preparations
Connect Gmail to look for RSVP replies and purchase confirmations
Set up and review a weekly Routine

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: 1. Pick up where we left off
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Open the planning chat and find the checklist you made in the previous lesson. Maybe you’ve ordered the decorations already, or picked up the cups on your way home. Add those updates first. We’re going to review this list, not create a new one each week.
Keep your manual updates in this chat. Replit can look for receipts, but it won’t know about the supplies sitting in your cupboard unless you tell it.

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: 2. Let’s connect Gmail
chunks.text:
Replit 101
We connected Google Calendar earlier. Now let’s add Gmail so Replit can find party replies and order confirmations. Open Integrations, search for Gmail, and follow the sign-in steps. Choose the right account and review the permissions before approving. You can also simply ask Replit to connect Gmail.
Finish connecting before scheduling the review, since a Routine can’t sign in for you. Use an account you’re allowed to connect. If you’re just practicing, you can use non-sensitive test messages or review the example without connecting. No purchases or real invitations are required.

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: 3. See how preparations are going
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Let’s try a quick check-in. In the chat with your checklist, ask Replit to look for this week’s purchase confirmations in Gmail and update your list.
Check my Gmail for items I purchased this week that are on our birthday checklist. Mark the matching items as ordered and show me the updated checklist with links to the confirmation emails.
Check the matches before moving on. “Ordered” means you’ve bought the item, not that it has arrived. If you bought something in person, tell Replit so it can update that too.

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: 4. Make it a weekly check-in
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Happy with the review? Let’s have Replit do this each week. In Replit, we call this creating a Routine. For example, every Thursday morning, Replit can check your purchase confirmations and update your checklist. Ask in the same chat so Replit knows which result you mean. If the party is tomorrow, try this with a later practice date so a weekly schedule makes sense.
I like this result. Can you please turn it into a routine and run it every Thursday morning?
Routines require a paid plan and available workspace access. If you’re not ready to activate one, that’s fine: you can review the proposal and run the check-in manually instead.

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: 5. Take a look inside your Routine
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Here’s an example of the proposal Replit shows before the weekly check-in starts. Let’s read it together: the Title names your Routine, Schedule says when it runs, and Prompt contains the instructions it will follow. You can review these before choosing Create routine. This card is a proposal, not proof that the Routine is already active.
Title: the screenshot uses “Birthday preparation review.” Choose a name you’ll recognize later.
Schedule: the example runs at 9 AM on Thursdays. The time-zone value is hidden in this image for privacy; check yours before confirming.
Prompt: check that the instructions repeat your purchase review using the right checklist, without buying anything or sending messages. This example also mentions RSVP replies and other possible checklist sources. Your checklist is in this chat, so you don’t need to connect Notion or Google Drive.
Per-run budget: no budget field is visible in this screenshot. Review the amount when it is presented during setup. It covers Replit carrying out one check-in, not shopping for party supplies or the entire series of weekly reviews.
Expected result: your updated checklist with links to the purchase confirmation emails, returned to this chat.
Create routine: confirm when the details are right, or choose Not now if you’re only exploring.
New routine proposal showing the Title, Thursday 9 AM Schedule, Prompt, Not now, and Create routine controls. The time-zone value is redacted.
Review the title, schedule, and instructions before creating the Routine. The time zone is redacted; no budget field is visible in this example.
/images/routine-setup/routine-proposal.webp

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: 6. Turn it on and follow your progress
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Happy with the details? Confirm the proposal when you’re ready to start. Then open Routines in the sidebar to find your check-in and review its schedule and activity. A proposal on its own is not an active Routine. Make sure Gmail access works before the first run; if a run gets stuck needing permission, come back to the chat to resolve it.
Check whether the Routine is enabled and when it is scheduled to run next.
After a run, check its activity and come back to this chat for the report and supporting email links.
Keep adding your own updates, especially purchases made in person.
If an email search fails or is incomplete, check again rather than assuming nothing has changed.
After the party, pause or delete the Routine. Recurring runs can use paid capacity.

chunks.title: Create a Routine
chunks.heading: A little less checking to do yourself
chunks.text:
Replit 101
You’ve gone from brainstorming a theme to finding supplies, making a checklist, and setting up a regular progress update. Gmail gives Replit the information to check; the Routine makes that check happen on a schedule. You still decide what to buy and who to contact. Replit helps you see what’s ready and what needs your attention next.

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
You’ve planned the birthday, picked a theme, and started getting everything ready. Now let’s impress your friends with a little RSVP app! Instead of sending just another message, you can share a party page where guests see the details and tell you if they’re coming.
Build a birthday RSVP app from a prompt
Test the guest experience and saved responses
Prepare your app to share with friends

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: 1. Imagine the invitation you’d love to share
chunks.text:
Replit 101
We chose a Pokémon theme earlier. Now imagine your friends opening the invitation, tapping a big Poké Ball, and choosing their favorite Pokémon as they RSVP. That’s the little app we’re going to build. You can use the same idea with your own theme, too.

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: 2. Start with a simple prompt
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Continue in your planning chat and ask Replit to build the app. It will move the app-building work into a project, where you can try it and keep improving it. We’ll start small, then add a couple of details with follow-up prompts.
Build a Pokémon-themed birthday RSVP app. Let guests tap a big Poké Ball to open the invitation, enter their name, and say if they’re coming. Make it playful and easy to use on a phone. Use fictional party details and don’t publish it yet.
Give Replit a little time to build, and answer any questions it asks. Then open Preview and tap the Poké Ball. Your version may look different from this example.
Edited example of a birthday app in Replit Preview with a park scene and a large Poké Ball. Personal names and location labels are replaced, avatars are generic, and the agent message is rewritten.
An example of the invitation screen, not an exact result guaranteed by the prompt. Identifying details and avatars have been replaced, and the agent message is edited for illustration.
/images/birthday-app/birthday-rsvp-example.webp

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: 3. Let guests choose a favorite Pokémon
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Now let’s make the RSVP a little more personal. Ask for one addition, then try it in Preview to see what changed.
Add a favorite Pokémon picker to the RSVP form, with Pikachu, Eevee, Charmander, Squirtle, Bulbasaur, and Mewtwo as choices.
Tap the Poké Ball, enter a made-up guest name, and choose a Pokémon. Check that your selection is clear and that all six choices are easy to use on a phone.

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: 4. Save the replies for the host
chunks.text:
Replit 101
A nice-looking form is a good start, but we also want to keep the replies. Ask Replit to save them and give you a private place to see who’s coming and which Pokémon they picked.
Save RSVPs and favorite Pokémon choices in a database. Add a private, sign-in-protected host page where only I can see the replies. Keep guest details hidden from other visitors.
Submit a test RSVP, then sign in as the host and check that the reply and Pokémon choice appear. Refresh to check that they were saved. In a signed-out browser window, verify that the host page and guest list are not accessible.

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: 5. Add a little celebration
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Let’s give your guests a fun finish. This is another small follow-up: keep what works and add one detail.
After an RSVP is saved, show a thank-you message with the guest’s chosen Pokémon and a little confetti. Respect reduced-motion settings and keep the existing RSVP features working.
Try another test reply. Check that the thank-you message shows the Pokémon you selected and that the response still appears in your private host view.

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: 6. Get ready to share with your friends
chunks.text:
Replit 101
When you’re happy with the app, review the party details and remove test responses before using it for real. Keep a child’s full name, photos, and home address off a public invitation page. Share any private location details separately with your guests. Test that only you can access the host view.
You can finish this lesson by testing in Preview. Publishing and sending the link are your next steps when you’re ready, not automatic actions.
When you choose to go live, use Publish in the project and review the publishing settings and any costs.
Open the published URL on your phone and test an RSVP again, including the favorite Pokémon picker. Confirm it appears in your private host view.
Share the published link with the people you want to invite. A link can be forwarded, so don’t treat it as private access control.
Replies in this app are stored in its database. They do not automatically update Google Calendar or appear in Gmail, so your Gmail Routine won’t see them unless you add that connection later.

chunks.title: Build your first app
chunks.heading: Your turn
chunks.text:
Help me check our birthday RSVP app before sharing it. Walk me through a test guest response, confirm it is saved, and help me verify that only the signed-in host can see the guest list. Don’t publish or send invitations yet.
I submitted test RSVPs and checked the saved responses as the host.
I checked the phone layout and verified that signed-out visitors cannot see the guest list.
I know publishing and sharing the link are separate decisions.

chunks.title: Explore different designs

Replit 101
Our birthday app is taking shape. But what if you’d like to try a different look? You don’t need to start again. Let’s open Design and explore a few alternatives on Canvas.
Find your app’s frames on Canvas
Use suggested next steps to explore alternatives
Choose a design that makes the RSVP easy to use

chunks.title: Explore different designs
chunks.heading: 1. Open Design
chunks.text:
Replit 101
In your app’s project, click Design at the top. This opens Canvas, a workspace where you can view designs as frames. A frame is a bounded preview of a screen or design. Start with the frame showing the birthday app we just created.
Design tab selected with the birthday invitation in a highlighted Canvas frame and suggested next steps alongside it. Identifying details and avatars are replaced.
Your app on Canvas. The outlined frame is the design you’re exploring. Personal details and photo avatars have been replaced.
/images/design-canvas/design-canvas.webp

chunks.title: Explore different designs
chunks.heading: 2. Hover to see suggested next steps
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Move your pointer over the app’s frame. Replit can suggest ways to explore it further, shown beside the frame under Suggested next steps. This is ambient intelligence: suggestions appear in the context of what you’re working on, so you don’t have to write a new prompt to get started.
Explore different approaches: try a fresh direction for the design.
Try different layouts: explore other ways to arrange the page.
Explore different vibes: try another visual mood.
More like this, but better: refine the direction you already have.
Canvas with a selected birthday app frame and suggestions to explore different approaches, layouts, vibes, or refinements. Personal details and avatars are replaced.
Hover over the frame to discover design suggestions. These are options to start an exploration, not the generated alternatives yet.

chunks.title: Explore different designs
chunks.heading: 3. Explore different approaches
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Click Explore different approaches and give Replit a little time to create alternatives. Compare the designs it presents. Maybe one makes the Poké Ball stand out more, while another gives the invitation a calmer background. Try a different suggestion if you want to focus on the layout or mood instead.

chunks.title: Explore different designs
chunks.heading: 4. Choose the one you like
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Select your favorite direction and tell Replit what you want to keep or refine. Think like a guest: can you read the party details and tell where to tap? A design should make the invitation easier to use, not just more colorful. When you’re ready to use it in the app, ask Replit to apply that direction while preserving the RSVP form, saved replies, and private host view. Then test those features again in Preview.
Exploring a design is not the same as publishing it. You decide when to apply changes and when to share the updated app. Next, we’ll create a supporting image on its own page.

chunks.title: Create assets

chunks.text:

You’ve found a look you like. Now let’s add a little surprise: an original Pokémon-inspired creature hidden in one of the trees! We’ll generate its image on Canvas, then ask Replit to add it to the app. An asset is something you use in a design, such as an illustration, background, or icon.

Canvas toolbar with Generate open and Image highlighted among Design, Image, Video, and Vector Graphic options. Identifying details and avatars are replaced.

For this example, we’re using Google’s Nano Banana, shown here as Nano Banana 2 Lite. Keep the square 1:1 shape and 1K size shown, then click the blue arrow to generate the image.
Create an original Pokémon-inspired forest creature called Mosskip: a tiny mint-green creature with leaf-shaped ears, an acorn cap, amber eyes, and a curled fern tail. Make it friendly and playful, with clean outlines that fit our illustrated park. Show the whole creature on a transparent background, with no text or scenery. Don’t copy an existing Pokémon.

Generated Mosskip creature with mint-green fur, leaf-shaped ears, an acorn cap, amber eyes, and a curled fern tail, shown on a checkerboard in Canvas.

Add the Mosskip image we just created to our birthday app, peeking out from behind one of the trees. When a guest taps it, show “You found Mosskip!” Make it a keyboard-accessible button too. Keep the Poké Ball, RSVP form, saved replies, and private host view working.

chunks.title: You’ve discovered Replit
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit 101
Congratulations! You’ve gone from a birthday-party idea to a working app, and explored several ways Replit can help along the way.
You started with a chat, brainstormed a Pokémon-themed party, connected your calendar, created an event, researched a shopping checklist, and set up a weekly routine.
Then you built a birthday invitation app, explored different designs, and created Mosskip, turning a generated image into an interactive surprise.
You’ve discovered Replit at the surface level. You don’t need to remember every control yet. Next, we’ll take a closer look at the places and tools you’ve already used.

chunks.title: You’ve discovered Replit

Replit 101
We’ll explore four short modules, one at a time:
Your workspace: understand where everything lives and how to find your work.
The prompt box: learn how to ask for what you need, add context, and choose models and modes.
Chats and projects: go deeper into when to use each, and how chats work inside projects.
Build and Design: explore how to build your app and develop its visual design.

chunks.title: You’ve discovered Replit

You’ve already moved between conversations, a project, and Canvas. Let’s start by understanding how those places fit together in your workspace.

chunks.title: Direct Agent effectively

chunks.text:
Work with Agent
Effective Agent work follows a reusable loop: define the outcome, provide relevant context, add constraints, inspect what happens, and refine the next step. This is more durable than memorizing prompt tricks.
Explain “Direct Agent effectively” in plain language
Using an outcome, context, constraints, inspection, and refinement loop
Apply the idea to one small, observable Replit outcome
Describe a small outcome to Agent, include what it should preserve, and state how you will check the result. Review the work and give one focused piece of feedback.

chunks.title: Direct Agent effectively
chunks.heading: Start with the big idea
chunks.text:
Work with Agent
Effective Agent work follows a reusable loop: define the outcome, provide relevant context, add constraints, inspect what happens, and refine the next step. This is more durable than memorizing prompt tricks.

chunks.title: Direct Agent effectively
chunks.heading: Why this is worth learning
chunks.text:
Work with Agent
Using an outcome, context, constraints, inspection, and refinement loop is the practical reason to learn this. It gives you a reusable way to collaborate with Agent across every Replit path. You provide direction and judgment; Agent helps investigate, create, and move the work forward. You are not here to memorize a term. You are learning when the idea can make an outcome clearer, safer, or more useful.

chunks.title: Direct Agent effectively
chunks.heading: Keep the first attempt manageable

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Your workspace
When you log into Replit, your workspace is your starting point. It brings together your chats, projects, and routines in one place.
Think of your workspace as the area where you organize your work and build your projects. You can start a conversation, return to an app you’re building, or find a routine you’ve set up.
In the previous module, you used these different parts to plan a birthday party and build an invitation app. Your workspace is where that work lives.

chunks.title: What is a Workspace?
chunks.heading: A place for your work
chunks.text:
Your workspace
Your workspace brings together several things you’ve already tried:
Chats: conversations where you explore ideas, ask questions, and get work done.
Projects: places where you build and keep developing apps and other creations.
Routines: recurring tasks you’ve set up to run on a schedule.

chunks.title: What is a Workspace?
chunks.heading: Your personal workspace
chunks.text:
Your workspace
A personal workspace is for your own work. Projects here belong to you, and you manage their sharing and visibility. Personal does not mean that everything you create must stay visible only to you: you can choose to share a project or publish an app.

chunks.title: What is a Workspace?
chunks.heading: A team workspace
chunks.text:
Your workspace
A team workspace is a shared place for an organization’s work. Projects here belong to the team rather than your personal workspace. Who can see or work on a project depends on the team’s permissions and sharing settings, so not every team member necessarily has access to every project.

chunks.title: What is a Workspace?
chunks.heading: Choose where your work belongs
chunks.text:
Your workspace
Use your personal workspace for your own projects and a team workspace for work that belongs to your team. Before starting a project, check which workspace you’re in. That choice helps determine who owns the project and how access is managed.
